approach:
To begin this lesson, ask students if they remember what a right-angle checker is. Show them the Explore task and ask them to use their checker (ruler) to identify the right angles in the picture in Explore. Ask them to show you which two lines meet to make the right angles. Explain that these two lines have a special name. Ask students if they know what the lines are called. Tell them they are called perpendicular lines. Can you identify any perpendicular lines in the classroom using your right-angle checkers? Guide students to realise that if they can find a right angle, they can find perpendicular lines.
Show students Master 3. Lead them to see that lines can be labelled using letters. In the example, we can say that line AB is perpendicular to line CD. Ask students what makes the lines perpendicular in Master 3 and 4, and what makes them not perpendicular. Are there things that must always be in place for lines to be perpendicular? Can short lines be perpendicular? Can thick lines be perpendicular? What matters most?
During Guided Practice, students are identifying perpendicular lines in a picture, angles and shapes.
formative_assessment:
understand that 'perpendicular' means two lines meet to make a right angle.
Students can use concrete materials to find and show perpendicular lines.
Students can identify perpendicular lines in a picture.
content_priority: This lesson can be completed by students independently.
national_curriculum: Identify and describe parallel and perpendicular lines, including those forming the sides of polygons.

approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task and ask them to discuss what they notice about the picture and the lines in the picture. Ask them how they would describe the beams going along the page in comparison to the beams pointing up. Are the lines perpendicular? What about the two beams pointing up? Are they perpendicular? What type of lines are they? Tell students that parallel lines are lines that do not make an angle, as they never meet, no matter how long they are. Let them know that perpendicular lines and parallel lines are special lines because of their unique characteristics. Ask them to identify these lines in the classroom.
Show students Master 2 and how to use arrow heads to indicate when lines are parallel.
During Guided Practice, students are identifying parallel lines in pictures, diagrams and shapes. For Example 2, ask them if they can prove that the lines EF and GH are not parallel. Illustrate that when the lines are extended, EF and GH will eventually meet to form an angle. Show them that even when lines AB and CD are extended, they will never meet. During Guided Practice 3, ask students to explain why they think certain lines are parallel. It can be difficult to check if lines are parallel 'by eye' so it is important students are able to justify their thinking by referring to the properties of parallel lines.
formative_assessment:
understand that parallel means two lines that never meet.
Students can use concrete materials to find and show parallel lines.
Students can identify parallel lines in a picture.
content_priority: This lesson can be completed by pupils independently.
national_curriculum: Identify and describe parallel and perpendicular lines, including those forming the sides of polygons.

approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task. Ask them to apply what they have learnt about special lines to describe the sides of the flip chart. Would it help if they label the lines? Show them how you would label the sides of the picture using A, B, C and D, as shown in Master 1. Allow them time to come up with descriptions of the lines.
Explain to students that there are other ways to describe lines. Tell them that we can also use the term 'vertical' to describe the lines. 'Vertical' lines are perpendicular to the floor. Can you identify the lines in the picture that are perpendicular to the floor? How many of these lines are there? Show them that the sides of the picture; the lines AC and BD, can be extended to show that they are perpendicular to the floor. What else can we say about these lines? Guide students to see that they are also parallel as they will never meet no matter how long they are extended.
Then ask students to describe lines AB and CD. They are parallel to each other. Guide students to see that they are also parallel to the floor, and tell them these lines are called 'horizontal' lines.
During Guided Practice, students are identifying horizontal and vertical lines in the classroom and in a picture.
formative_assessment:
understand the term 'horizontal', meaning parallel to the floor.
Students can identify the term 'vertical', meaning perpendicular to the floor.
Students can use concrete materials to identify horizontal and vertical lines.
Students can identify horizontal and vertical lines in a picture.
content_priority: This lesson can be completed by students independently.

objective: describe a 2D shape using angle and side properties.
approach:
To begin this lesson, provide students with a 2D trapezoid as shown in the Explore task. Ask them to describe the shape using what they have learnt about angles and lines. Ask them to start with angles. How many are there in the shape? What types of angles are they? How do they know? Can they label all the angles in the shape?
Then ask students to describe the sides. How many sides does the shape have? What do we call such a shape? Can we label the sides? What kind of lines do the sides make? Can you mark out the lines? Explain to students that we can describe and identify all types of shapes using their angle and side properties, as they have just done.
During Guided Practice, students are describing each of the shapes using the familiar vocabulary identified during the Explore task.
formative_assessment:
Pupils can identify angles in a 2D shape.
Pupils can name the angles in a 2D shape.
Pupils can identify the vertices in a 2D shape.
Pupils can identify the sides of a 2D shape.
Pupils can describe the sides using 'perpendicular' and 'parallel'.
content_priority: This lesson can be completed if time allows.
national_curriculum:

Identify, classify, and describe the attributes of polygons (including triangles and quadrilaterals) using properties of shapes, including line and rotational symmetry.

approach:
To begin this lesson, provide students with 1 cm square grid paper. Show them the Explore task and ask them which shape is smaller. Tell them your friend can clearly see that the rectangle is smaller. Is this true? How can we be sure? Allow students to draw the shapes to scale on their grid paper and compare them. They can cut them out to compare directly. Ask them to think of other ways to compare the shapes. Show them they can also compare by counting the number of squares within each shape.
During Guided Practice, students are drawing 2D shapes to scale using square grid paper and a ruler.
formative_assessment:
use square grid paper to draw 2D shapes.
Students can use a ruler to draw 2D shapes.
Students can follow directions about length and width when drawing a 2D shape.
Students can compare 2D shapes that have been drawn on square grid paper.

approach:
To begin this lesson, provide students with nets that have been cut out and partially folded. Have the students work in pairs to fold the nets into 3D shapes. Can they match the nets they have to the nets shown in the Explore task? Ask how they knew Meilani's box was not the first shape shown in the Explore task.
With the three shapes they have constructed, ask where they will find the properties of the shapes that will allow them to complete the table in Master 4.
During Guided Practice, students are naming familiar 3D shapes and matching nets with 3D shapes. For Example 2, students should have access to the nets of the different shapes so that they are able to fold and unfold them to make the connection between the nets and the completed shapes.
formative_assessment:

Students can identify the correct net for a 3D shape by building them or describing them.
Students can identify the features of 3D shapes, using terms such as 'faces', 'vertices' and 'sides'.
Students can identify the 2D shapes on 3D shapes.

approach:
To begin this lesson, provide each student with some play dough. Show them the Explore task and ask them to make a model of the box. What kind of shape is the box? How many faces does the box have? What is the 2D shape of each face? Lead students to recall that this is a cuboid. It is made up of 6 rectangles. Guide them to use the properties of a cuboid to help them make the 3D shape using play dough.
Next, ask students to cut the cuboid in four parts (or cut the cuboid to show them). What do they notice? The four parts are identical. Can we change the cuboid into a sphere? Do you remember what a sphere is? Can you describe it? Then ask them to cut it in half (or cut the sphere to show them). What do you notice about the two sides?
During Guided Practice, students are drawing a cube and a prism. Allow them to discuss the difference between these two shapes.
formative_assessment:
use concrete materials to build 3D shapes.
Students can identify the features of 3D shapes, using terms such as 'faces', 'vertices' and 'sides'.
Students can identify the 2D shapes on 3D shapes.
Students can identify 3D shapes that have symmetrical sides.

approach:
To begin this lesson, provide students with a cuboid. Ask them how many edges it has. Tell them that the edges of a cuboid are lines. How can we describe the edges using what we have learnt about lines? Ask students to use their finger to trace the lines as they describe them. Prompt them with vocabulary they have learnt in previous lessons, including 'perpendicular', 'parallel', 'horizontal' and 'vertical'.
During Guided Practice, students are looking at irregular objects to identify horizontal and vertical lines.
formative_assessment:
use the terms 'parallel' and 'perpendicular' to describe the edges of a 3D shape.
Students can use the terms 'horizontal' and 'vertical' to describe the edges of a 3D shape.
Students can label the edges of a 3D shape and identify them as lines.
